Q: Access Attribute of Rails Test Fixture in Associated FixtureSet A:

How to access Associated Fixture Sets:

Taken from Fizzy (publicly available).

# users.yml
david:
  id: <%= ActiveRecord::FixtureSet.identify("david", :uuid) %>
  name: David
  role: member
  identity: david
  account: 37s_uuid  # <------ notice this here
  verified_at: <%= Time.current.to_fs(:db) %>

Source: https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/main/test/fixtures/users.yml

Notice the key-value entry for account?

# Let's review the accounts.yml file
37s:
  id: <%= ActiveRecord::FixtureSet.identify("37s", :uuid) %>  # < ---- check this out
  name: 37signals
  external_account_id: <%= ActiveRecord::FixtureSet.identify("37signals") %>
  cards_count: 5

Source: https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/main/test/fixtures/accounts.yml

That's how you can reference via label - they're using UUIDs. But I prefer simply using the label name.

Docs

Checkout out the section: "Stable, Autogenerated IDs" in the following link: https://api.rubyonrails.org/v8.0.1/classes/ActiveRecord/FixtureSet.html

Q: How to sort a PySpark dataframe rows by the order of a list? A:

Use an enumeration of your list as a sorting column and join key:

from pyspark.sql.functions import col
index_df = spark.createDataFrame([(index, val) for index, val in enumerate(col_A_itm_order)], ['index', 'col_a'])

ordered_df = your_df.alias('a')\
.join(index_df.alias('b'), on = 'col_a')\
.orderBy('index')\
.select(col('a.*'))

Hope this helps anyone else who ended up here for silly spreadsheet report requirement reasons.

Q: Nested dictionary output A:

I'm assuming you're using this package (not totally sure since your code doesn't quite look like the code shown here). Therefore, I'm looking at the structure shown near the bottom of this page. Because this dictionary has inconsistent structure, it will be difficult to iterate through in one clean loop. But since you know the structure and the key names, you can pull out what you want by just using the names of the keys and iterating through each list/dictionary you want to look at individually.

For example, getting the dict for every TCP connection, then iterating through those dictionaries:

tcp_nested_dict = results[ip]["tcp"]

#translates to: for key, value in dict, but renamed for clarity
#the key is the port id
for port_id, info_dict in tcp_nested_dict:
    for key, value in info_dict:
        #your code here

Please note that this code won't work for going through every item in the dict. For example, it won't work for results[ip]["portused"], because that corresponds to a list of dicts, not another dict.

If you want to go through everything at once, it might be possible with iterators, but it'd be real fussy since this data structure isn't consistently organized. I don't think I would recommend this. There isn't that much stuff in the dictionary, and it's all clearly labeled, so just access the labels you want by using the key names. This will also be more legible.

NOTE: You might not need to use the nested dict at all. It seems like you can also get the nm info as a csv, like this:

nm = nmap.PortScanner()
nm.scan(ip)
print(nm.csv()) #this will just print the csv so you can see it -- eventually, you will probably want to save it or put it into a dataframe.

If the goal is to extract information and save it, this latter option is probably the better choice. But it would depend on exactly what info you wanted and what format you wanted it in.

Q: How to do a python range with offset A:

Assuming your question is about offsetting a range at run time after it has been created, and when you don't have the parameters used for its creation. The solution is to retrieve the range attributes. A new object must be created since range is immutable.

The initial range:

a, b, step = 4, 20, 3
r = range(a, b, step)
print(r)

The new offset range:

offset = 10
r2 = range(r.start+offset, r.stop+offset, r.step)
print(r2)

range(4, 20, 3)
range(14, 30, 3)

An alternate method is to offset the materialized elements of a range with map using the currently selected answer, but you lose the generator nature of a range, for a range with numerous elements this can be a problem.

Q: MySQL insert with the current timestamp A:

You need to use now() (instead of 'now') as you are looking for the function and not for the string.

Q: Auto update DATETIME column on insert with SQL? A:

For most SQL dialects, you can use a DATETIME column with a default of current_timestamp. That handles creation.

create table whatever (
    ...
    updated datetime default current_timestamp
);

Then add an after update trigger.

create trigger foo_updated
after update
on foo
for each row
begin
    update foo set updated = current_timestamp where id = new.id;
end;

MySQL has some special syntax to do this. You can make the trigger in your create table statement with an with an on update.

create table whatever (
    ...
    updated datetime default current_timestamp on update current_timestamp
);

And then there's MySQL's timestamp date type. Timestamp will set itself to the current date and time anytime a row is updated... sorta.

The rules are very complicated which is why it's better to use datetime and on update.
